explanations.explanation: Verse 15 says it plainly: “…each according to his own ability.” So five, two and one were not a lucky draw. Nobody got a number pulled out of a hat. The master looked at each servant and handed over an amount to match.

explanations.answer: How long each one has served
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd think so, since that's how a lot of workplaces run. But the passage never mentions anybody's years of service. It says the amounts went “…each according to his own ability.” Nobody here gets a bigger pile for having the oldest name tag.

Nobody in this story is elbowing to the front of the line. The text never says anyone asked for anything. The master simply gave, “…each according to his own ability.” It's not a race to the cookie box, friend.

Verse 16 says he “…went at once and put them to work and gained five more.” Five he was given, five he gained. That puts him at ten talents total, and you'll hear that number again before the passage is over. He doubled what he had.

Ten is a real number in this story, so I get the mix-up. But ten is what he ends up holding, not what he gained. Five he started with plus five he gained makes ten. It's five more, friend, and the math works out.

One talent is what the third servant was handed, so that's a different man. The five-talent servant is the one in this verse. The text says he gained five more. That's a full doubling, and he got there by putting the money to work.
Verse 17 says, “Likewise, the one with the two talents gained two more.” Two in, two more out. That makes four, a full doubling, same as the first servant. Smaller pile, same result.

It's true, actually. Verse 17 says, “Likewise, the one with the two talents gained two more.” He was given two and gained two more, so he ends up with four. That's the same kind of result the five-talent servant got.

explanations.answer: Digs a hole and hides it
explanations.explanation: Verse 18 says he “…dug a hole in the ground, and hid his master’s money.” That's it. That's the whole plan. The other two servants were out putting the money to work, and he was out digging a hole.

Spending would at least be a plan with some excitement in it, but the text doesn't say that. He hid the money. Later he hands it back with the words “See, you have what belongs to you.” (Matthew 25:25) You can't hand back what you already spent.

explanations.answer: Gives it away to the poor
explanations.explanation: The passage never says he gave anything to anybody. Verse 18 says he “…dug a hole in the ground, and hid his master’s money.” Hiding it is what the text says he did. I think a hole in the ground is a lonely place for a talent.

Verse 19 says otherwise: “After a long time the master of those servants returned and settled accounts with them.” It was a long time, not a quick trip to the store. The servants had plenty of days to decide what to do with what they were given.

Right, it's false. Verse 19 says, “After a long time the master of those servants returned…” He was gone a good while. Long enough that waiting got to be part of the job, and that goes for every servant.

Verse 21 says, “You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things.” A few things was the starting point. Many things is where it leads. The master doesn't hand this servant a little pat on the back.

Fewer would be a strange reward, like getting a promotion to a smaller office. The master says the opposite: “You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things.” (Matthew 25:21) The servant goes up from here.

Nothing in the master's words says simpler. He says, “You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things.” It's about how much, not how easy. I think this servant is about to be very busy.

explanations.answer: It's word for word the same
explanations.explanation: Put verse 21 next to verse 23 and they match exactly. Both servants hear, “Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!” The two-talent servant had a smaller pile, and he got the very same words. The size of the pile didn't change the praise.

explanations.answer: It praises him a little less
explanations.explanation: I get it, two is less than five, so you'd figure the praise shrinks too. But check verse 23 and you won't find one word taken out. It's the same “Well done, good and faithful servant!” the first servant heard. Not a crumb missing.

explanations.answer: It comes with a stern warning
explanations.explanation: No warning for this servant. Verse 23 is the same warm reply the five-talent servant got, ending with “Enter into the joy of your master!” The stern words come in this parable, but they go to a different servant. This one walks away with only good news.

That's the word he uses. In verse 25 he says, “So I was afraid and went out and hid your talent in the ground.” Notice that's his own explanation, told to the master's face. Fear was the reason he gave for the hole.

Ashamed is a decent guess, but it's not the word he picked. He says, “So I was afraid and went out and hid your talent in the ground.” Nothing in his speech mentions shame. The word out of his mouth is afraid.
He doesn't say angry. Verse 25 has him saying, “So I was afraid and went out and hid your talent in the ground.” He doesn't mention anger at all. The word he gives the master is afraid.

I can see why you'd think so, since the money did come back in one piece. But the master's answer is “You wicked, lazy servant!” That's not a pat on the back. Hiding the talent in the ground wasn't what the master was looking for.

That's right. The master's reply in verse 26 begins, “You wicked, lazy servant!” Keeping the money safe didn't win any praise from him. Burying dough in a hole doesn't make it rise, and the master noticed.

Verse 27 says, “Then you should have deposited my money with the bankers, and on my return I would have received it back with interest.” The master names the bankers and the interest. It was a simple step, and the servant skipped it.

Giving to the poor isn't what the master says here. He says the servant “…should have deposited my money with the bankers…” The money was the master's, and he says what to do with it. The bankers are the answer, and the interest would have come with them.

A field is a nice idea, but the master never brings one up. Verse 27 says, “Then you should have deposited my money with the bankers…” So the answer was the bankers. It would have come back with interest.

explanations.answer: The one who has ten talents
explanations.explanation: Verse 28 says, “Therefore take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents.” That's the servant who started with five and gained five more. The one talent goes to the servant who already has the biggest pile.

explanations.answer: The one who has four talents
explanations.explanation: Four is the right number for the two-talent servant, who gained two more. Good thinking on the math. But the master doesn't send the talent to him. He says, “…give it to the one who has ten talents.”

The master doesn't name a steward here. He names the receiver by his count: “…the one who has ten talents.” That's the first servant, the one who put his five to work and gained five more. Verse 28 has the master say it plainly.

Yes, and it's a hard line. Verse 29 says, “But the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.” The master says it right after he explains the first half, that everyone who has will be given more. Both halves come from the same verse.

It's true, though it's a tough one to hear. Verse 29 says, “But the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.” The master says it as the reason for giving the one talent away. It goes right alongside the line about being given more.

Verse 30 says, “And throw that worthless servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” I think this is a heavy part, and it should be read slowly. It's where the master's words end.
There's no prison in this verse. The master says, “And throw that worthless servant into the outer darkness…” I think this is a heavy part of the story. It's worth reading just as it's written.

The text doesn't send the servant to a far country. Verse 30 says he is thrown “…into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” I think this is a heavy verse, so let's take it as it is.
